note: M1. Core fork: von Neumann search (game-playing, utility maximization) vs Simon search / means-ends analysis (structuring an ill-defined problem). means-ends analysis + satisficing + heuristic are load-bearing for the product's Sequencer.

entities.name: search
entities.definition: Dividing the labor of a complex problem into plans (sequences of actions) and using heuristics to economize on information processing — generating and evaluating only satisfactory plans rather than testing every state.

entities.name: search tree
entities.definition: A state space drawn as nodes (states) and paths (action sequences); a highly restricted network whose only links are sequential. Agents transition from an initial state to a goal state through it.

entities.name: heuristic
entities.definition: An imperfect but stable rule-of-thumb that guides which actions/plans to generate-and-test and which to ignore, pruning branches of the search tree to economize on processing.

entities.name: satisficing
entities.definition: Simon's heuristic of searching only for a satisfactory plan that crosses an aspiration level, then stopping — rather than optimizing or maximizing rewards.

entities.name: von Neumann search
entities.definition: Search conceived as playing a well-defined, often adversarial game (chess, checkers, Go): states reduce to numerical utility and are evaluated by a heuristic evaluation function. Extends reinforcement learning and Shannon information.

entities.name: means-ends analysis
entities.definition: Simon search (Newell & Simon's General Problem Solver): treat the difference between the current state and the goal state as intermediate feedback, and invoke an operator linked to that difference to get closer to the goal.

entities.name: utility function
entities.definition: A function mapping each game state to a numerical expected reward (the 'utility'), estimated via a heuristic evaluation function so alternative actions can be ranked without searching the whole tree.

entities.name: John von Neumann
entities.definition: Mathematician whose game theory underlies search as adversarial game-playing with utility functions.

relations.evidence: Search divides the labor of a complex problem using heuristics to assign credit more efficiently.
Agents search by generating and selecting plans using heuristics.
Satisficing is itself a heuristic governing when to stop searching.
Heuristics 'prune' branches, avoiding evaluation of every state in a combinatorially explosive tree.
Heuristics guide which parts of the search tree to generate-and-test.
Von Neumann search is search conceived as game-playing.
Simon search is search conceived as means-ends analysis.
States are collapsed into a single utility value via an evaluation function.
Samuel's checkers program used reinforcement learning to improve the evaluation function.
Simon search manipulates physical symbols (lists) toward a meaningful goal state.
Simon search structures an open-ended problem, closer to learning-in-a-society.
The difference between current and goal state is the intermediate feedback that invokes an operator.
The inverted stacked-maze tree looks like Minsky's hierarchical 'society' (CEO/managers/staff).

claims.proposition: Search is a heuristic process: dividing a complex problem into plans and using heuristics to generate-and-test only satisfactory plans, by contrast to brute force which tests every state.
The division of labor is a general solution to credit assignment: any complex task can be divided into simpler subtasks that are easier to learn and can be mechanized.
Using heuristics to prune branches of the search tree lets an agent solve a combinatorially explosive problem by evaluating only parts of the tree, economizing on information processing.
claims.conditions: the problem is not random (heuristics must carry real information)

claims.proposition: Intelligent agents satisfice: they search only for satisfactory plans crossing an aspiration level and then stop, rather than seeking optimal plans or maximizing rewards.
claims.conditions: information processing is costly and goals are organizational/ambiguous

claims.proposition: Von Neumann search treats search as a well-defined game: every state is collapsed into a numerical utility via an evaluation function, and reinforcement learning improves that function.

Simon search (means-ends analysis) treats the difference between the current and goal state as feedback that invokes an operator; with a good representation the goal state may already be implicit in the initial state, requiring no search.
claims.conditions: the world is open-ended and must be represented

tensions.dimension: what 'search' is: playing a well-defined game by maximizing a utility function vs. understanding and structuring an ill-defined problem by reducing differences toward a meaningful goal
tensions.conditions_a: Von Neumann search fits when the rules and goals are well-defined and often adversarial (chess, Go, checkers): all states reduce to a numerical utility, so reinforcement learning over an evaluation function suffices and physical symbols are unnecessary.
tensions.conditions_b: Simon search fits when the world is open-ended and the problem itself must be represented: search becomes the manipulation of physical symbols (lists) toward a meaningful goal state via means-ends analysis, where a good representation can dissolve the search entirely.

probes.prompt: Why is 'search' called search rather than brute force? Explain how heuristics and satisficing together let an agent solve a combinatorially explosive problem without examining the whole search tree.
expected_signals: Contrasts search with brute force: heuristics let the agent evaluate only part of the tree rather than every state.
Explains heuristics as rules-of-thumb that prune branches, economizing on information processing.
Explains satisficing as stopping once a plan crosses an aspiration level, rather than finding the optimum.
Notes this trades a guarantee of optimality for tractability — satisfactory, not optimal, solutions.
